Marc Davis  [12:34 PM]
@channel OK, I drove it. Definitely still vibration, though. I used the vibration app on my phone on the floor of the car and found two peaks. One at 12Hz and one at 24Hz when I was driving at about 50 mph. These tires turn 870 revs per mile so, at 50mph, that's about 725rpm. 725rpm/60 seconds = 12Hz.  If it were driveshaft vibration, it would be at 4.1x wheel speed which is 2972rpm and about 49.5Hz.  So, I believe we are dealing with wheel vibration here

Let's have our best shop re-balance these wheels @Ryan Laurel and, if it's still there, we can tell Pat that we can try to get a set of these but no guarantee that they'll be perfect either:

www.niemoeller.de/en/w180/w180/B010/26/c40004-disc-wheel-with-drop-centre-rim-5jx13 
 from our collective brain:
The two cursors land on two different things.
Cursor 1 at 11.8 Hz = 708 rpm. That's your wheel/tire rotation. At 50 mph and 870 rev/mile you computed 725 rpm = 12.1 Hz, so 11.8 Hz is dead-on (within speedometer/tire-circumference slop). This is first-order tire/wheel imbalance — a heavy spot or out-of-balance wheel hitting once per revolution. It shows up strongest on X (fore-aft) and Z, consistent with an imbalance/uniformity issue.
Cursor 2 at 23.7 Hz = 2× the wheel frequency, the second harmonic. A peak at exactly twice rotation speed is the classic signature of tire/wheel non-uniformity — radial force variation, out-of-round, a flat spot, or a mounted-tire/rim runout that produces two bumps per revolution. It's the dominant peak in your X trace, which fits a radial uniformity problem felt as a fore-aft/vertical shake.
So what's going on: you've got a wheel-speed-order vibration. 1st order (11.8 Hz) points to imbalance, and a strong 2nd order (23.7 Hz) points to tire uniformity / out-of-round / runout. Both scale with vehicle speed, so the give-away test is to drive at a different speed — both peaks should slide proportionally (e.g., at 60 mph they'd move to ~14.2 and ~28.4 Hz). If they move with speed, it's rotational and not engine/driveline-fixed or structural resonance.
A couple of things worth checking to confirm and narrow it down:
The smaller red bump near ~3 Hz (around 180 rpm) — too slow for the tire; could be a driveshaft or half-shaft order depending on your axle ratio, or body/suspension hop. Worth identifying since your build has a custom driveline.
Whether the 23.7 Hz peak dominates over 11.8 Hz (it does here, in X) suggests the uniformity/out-of-round issue is the bigger contributor to what you feel than raw imbalance.
Practical next step: road-force balance or at least a spin balance plus a runout check on the worst wheel. If balancing kills the 11.8 Hz but leaves 23.7 Hz, the tire itself (or the rim) has a uniformity defect and may need to be re-indexed on the rim or replaced.

well ... i went deeper ... and told it "this really only happens around 50mph" ... and the answer is quite interesting (if true)

Here's the distinction. Imbalance and uniformity peaks (your 11.8 and 23.7 Hz) are always present; their amplitude grows smoothly with speed and never has a "sweet spot" where it gets bad and then better. What you're describing — bad at 50, better on either side — means that at 50 mph, a rotational forcing frequency is lining up with the natural frequency of some part of the car, and that part is ringing.
At 50 mph your tire turns at 11.8 Hz (1st order) and the 2nd order sits at 23.7 Hz. One of those is almost certainly coinciding with a structural resonance:
23.7 Hz is a very typical tire/suspension hop or wheel-hop resonance (unsprung mass on the tire/suspension spring rate usually lands in the 12–18 Hz range, but bushing-stiffened or heavier custom setups push higher). It's also right in the band for many driveshaft bending modes and subframe modes.
The fact that the 23.7 Hz peak is the dominant one in your X trace, and the symptom is speed-specific, strongly suggests the 2nd tire order is exciting a structure that resonates around there.
So the mechanism: the tire's 2nd-order force (from uniformity/out-of-round) is the exciter, and something on the car has a natural frequency near 23.7 Hz that amplifies it. Off 50 mph, the forcing frequency walks away from the resonance and the amplitude drops. That's why it's a 50 mph phenomenon and not a 40 or 60 phenomenon.

Connolly 220S — vibration diagnosis (July 7)
Diagnostic steps taken today:
Re-measured vibration after roadforce balancing + re-clocking the wheels. The 2nd-order "out-of-round wheel" signature dropped ~75% (wheels were a real, now largely-fixed contributor), but a once-per-rev (1st-order) vibration remained and became dominant. Balancing can't touch that, so it points inboard to the hub/flange — matching Dave's damaged pass-rear flange reading .007–.009" lateral runout.
Cleared a separate scraping noise: cotter-pin wire diameter too small, letting the spring keeper rub inside the drum. Confirmed the flange damage was pre-existing (visible in earlier brake-work photos).
Jackstand test, driveline spun bare (no wheels/tires/drums, ~55–60 mph equiv): pulling the wheels + drums removed ~70% of total vibration (0.110 → 0.031 g). Confirmed most of it lives at the wheel/tire/drum/flange interface, but exposed a smaller driveshaft 1st-order residual (~0.013 g) that wheel work won't fix.
Axle isolation test, each rear axle spun alone (open diff, opposite side held): right axle threw a big once-per-rev shake (0.039 g) vs the left (0.002 g) — ~20x worse. A clean 1st order like that is the signature of a bent/eccentric right rear axle shaft or flange.
Final conclusion: the right rear axle is bent — that's the residual vibration source; the left axle is good. It's one axle, not the pair, so the ~$7,500 German set isn't needed. Plan: confirm with a dial indicator (right vs. left as reference), re-face the flange for brake-drum seating, and source/refurbish a used right axle. Next steps: order a 2nd-hand right axle plus wheel bearing, pull the RH axle and take both to a machine shop; if the old one measures true, the issue is deeper in the diff (possibly u-joint). Colvin's was called for input before pulling on-site.

Got another vibration measurement at 60mph. Marc put into Claude. Results:
U-joint / ride-height experiment — it split the problem in two
Re-ran the right-axle jackstand test, but this time loaded the car so the swing-axle U-joint was straight (yesterday it was bent because unloaded).
Confirmed — U-joint angle drives the 2nd-order vibration. A Cardan joint at an angle makes a twice-per-rev shake. Straightening it dropped the 2nd-order component 87% (0.0083 → 0.0011 g). So ride height genuinely matters — setting/holding correct static ride height removes a real chunk of vibration. Cheap win.
But the main defect is 1st-order and it did NOT move. The right axle's once-per-rev shake stayed put (0.042 → 0.035 g, within speed variation). A U-joint angle can't cause a 1st-order — that's a bent shaft / eccentric flange / imbalance. So the joint isn't the cause of the big one; it's mechanical, and it travels with the right axle.
Road implication worth noting: on the road the U-joint's 2nd-order lands at ~29 Hz — the same frequency we've been calling "out-of-round wheel." So part of that stubborn 28.6 Hz on the road was probably the U-joint running at an angle, which is why roadforce balancing never fully killed it. Fixing ride height should take another bite out of it.
Two separable issues on the right rear now:
1. U-joint operating angle (ride height) — real, 2nd-order, fixable by geometry. Set + verify static ride height. Experiment shows it works.
2. Right axle 1st-order defect — bent shaft / eccentric joint flange (part 27) / imbalance. This is the main event. Dial-indicate the right axle shaft + flange runout vs the left as reference, and check the U-joint (part 6) for wear/play while we're in there.
Caveat: jackstand spins the right axle at 2x road speed, so it exaggerates the 1st-order force ~4x. Real defect, but the road contribution is more modest than the number here (it's the ~14 Hz road residual, ~0.03 g).
Plan: dial in ride height, then measure/address the right axle shaft + flange runout. New wheels still won't touch either of these.

Work performed
The right rear axle and a new wheel bearing were ordered first thing. Marc's ride-height experiment split the vibration in two: straightening the U-joint angle killed the 2nd-order shake by 87% (fixable via ride height), but the main 1st-order defect stayed — a mechanical fault traveling with the right axle. David then inspected the internal U-joint and found it clearly bad: excessive play, lash, witness marks, notchiness. He made the car drivable again (gear oil, parking brake, wheels torqued). Jordan mapped the parts across German fiches (sliding joint 1803500513, U-joint 111 350 00 28, sliding sleeve, shims) — ~$1,600 to rebuild, or ~$450 for a used U-joint — and located a needed special tool.
Communications made
Internally, the team agreed to call Casey at Colvin's for a removal/rebuild plan; Jordan noted he'd specifically asked Colvin's to check this joint during the original rebuild and it apparently wasn't. Externally, you sent two supplier emails: one to Jelinek ("1959 220S") asking for part 53/53A from a rear-axle diagram, and one to Niemöller ("W180 rear axle sliding joint compatibility question") asking them to confirm sliding sleeve 180 350 07 13 fits your car.
Conclusions
Two separable issues: a ride-height/U-joint angle component (fixable by geometry) and the main 1st-order defect, now pinned largely on a worn internal U-joint that should have been caught in the prior rebuild. "Installed rear shocks.
Attempted to adjust rear ride height.
Issues with vintage v-dubs IRS kit were discovered when attempting to adjust rear ride height.
Welds failing on swing plates adjustment blocks.
Torsion bar side of the adjustable swing plate not properly constrained to the backing plate, causing the plates to walk apart as the suspension moved. When I adjusted the screw this time it actually split the two apart completely. From the marks on the adjuster plate it looks to have been walking for a while.

Did a bunch of research to determine the best path going forward. Remove spring plates. Straighten the plate and re-weld the adjustment blocks.
Add constraining hardware to ensure the two-part plate can't pull apart. The slot is there, but no matching stud or thread on the companion plate. Looking around it does appear to be something most high-quality kits do.
Add a bushing to the torsion bar cap to press the two plates together. This wasn't included in the kit but Aharon confirmed it's a necessity.
Install a longer adjustment screw to give us a little more height.
Regarding the shock mounting, I believe one of the many parts that were missing from the kit was upper shock mounts which were likely to prevent this contact. Where the shock mounts were intended to go I'm not sure. I moved the spacers around to create maximum clearance, and it appears that currently it will not make contact at full droop. Ryan brought the bus back from Soulspeed today reporting another inverter overtemp "limp mode" — an issue we hadn't seen in weeks since switching the reservoir return line from 3/8" to 5/8". I verified the basics first: coolant reservoir full and flowing well, no bubbles, and the coolant fan operating.
A few observations from digging in: the inlet and outlet are swapped on the inverter (probably doesn't matter, but we could set it to Tesla spec), and we run the inverter and motor in series while Tesla actually plumbs them in parallel. Neither seems likely to fix the inverter temp, but both are options to test.
I ran two controlled test drives at 100°F ambient to isolate whether airflow (the skidplate) is the culprit.
Run 1 (skidplate on): inverter started at 109°F and hit the 160°F overtemp limp mode after 13 minutes of hard-ish driving. Motor climbed from 163°F to 232°F — still mid-gauge in the Ampere GUI. Notably, the temperature creep is slow and steady, not "peaky" like Connolly was with its restrictive return line (30°F swings with throttle); Ferdman barely reacts to power input or off-throttle periods.
Run 2 (skidplate removed): inverter started at 104°F, motor at 165°F. Took 17 minutes / 2.5 laps of the same loop to hit limp mode at 160°F inverter, 241°F motor.
Conclusion: removing the skidplate bought roughly 25% more time/distance before limp mode, but didn't prevent it. Airflow is a contributing factor, not the root cause. Next candidates to test: correcting the inverter inlet/outlet to Tesla spec and re-plumbing the motor/inverter from series to parallel.

from 7/16:
spent the day deliberating and choosing a path forward.
I ended up straightening all the bent plates from the drivers side
Then tapping both slide plates to m12 so we can have a better clamping force.
While installing the torsion plates, I evened both sides at 9cm- spring plate to corner of the housing. I then preloaded the arms while sliding them in and securing.
After that I could pull the arms over to meet the slide plates and realign to the previous spots.
This method insures our "lowest" ride height is also the lowest position on the adjuster, now we can go way up if we want.
After we decide we like our ride height, we will remove the wheels and add 2 extra bolts towards the end of the spring plates, that way we can lock it down permanently and not worry about the plates deforming any more.
